overview:
In Jainism, the Twenty-four Tirthankaras are the exemplary liberated teachers of the present descending time-cycle (avasarpini). The term “Tirthankara” literally means a maker of a ford (tīrtha) across saṃsāra—the endless cycle of birth and death. A Tirthankara is not a creator-god but a perfected soul (jina, arihanta) who has destroyed all karmic bondage, attained kevala-jñāna (omniscience), and then re-establishes the fourfold community (saṅgha) of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Through their teaching and personal example, they show how right faith (samyag-darśana), right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), and right conduct (samyag-cāritra) lead to mokṣa, the final liberation of the soul.

Jain cosmology describes time as beginningless and cyclical, divided into ascending (utsarpini) and descending (avasarpini) half-cycles. In each half-cycle, twenty-four Tirthankaras appear. The Twenty-four Tirthankaras of the current avasarpini begin with Ṛṣabhanātha (also called Ādinātha, the “first lord”) and culminate in Mahāvīra, whose historical life in the 6th century BCE is relatively well documented. Between them are Ajitanātha, Sambhavanātha, Abhinandananātha, Sumatinātha, Padmaprabhu, Suparśvanātha, Candraprabhu, Suvidhinātha (Puṣpadanta), Śītalanātha, Śreyāṃsanātha, Vasupūjya, Vimalanātha, Anantanātha, Dharmanātha, Śāntinātha, Kunthunātha, Arahanātha, Mallinātha, Naminātha, Neminātha (Aristanemi), Pārśvanātha, and finally Mahāvīra. Each is associated with a distinctive symbol (lāñchana)—such as the bull for Ṛṣabha, the snake-hood for Pārśva, and the lion for Mahāvīra—which appears beneath their images in temples and helps identify them in iconography.

Traditional narratives, especially in texts like the Kalpa Sūtra and various Purāṇa-type Jain works, describe the birth, renunciation, austerities, enlightenment, and liberation (nirvāṇa) of each Tirthankara. These accounts emphasize their extraordinary compassion and their role in re-establishing dharma whenever spiritual decline has obscured the path. For example, Ṛṣabhanātha is portrayed as teaching early humans agriculture, crafts, and social organization, thereby founding an ordered society before renouncing the world. Pārśvanātha is remembered for emphasizing four vows—non-violence, truth, non-stealing, and non-possession—which Mahāvīra later systematizes into the well-known five great vows (mahāvrata) by adding celibacy.

From a doctrinal perspective, the Twenty-four Tirthankaras embody the Jain ideal that liberation is achieved through self-effort rather than divine grace. They are born as human beings, accumulate special “Tirthankara-nāma-karma” in previous lives, and then, in their final birth, realize perfect knowledge and conduct. Their lives illustrate the progressive purification of the soul through the fourteen stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna), culminating in the complete destruction of ghātiyā karmas (knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding, and energy-obstructing karmas). Once liberated, they no longer intervene in worldly affairs, but their teachings, preserved in scriptures and living traditions, continue to guide aspirants.

Historically, Mahāvīra and, to a lesser extent, Pārśvanātha are the most accessible figures for modern scholarship, with inscriptional and textual evidence from early centuries BCE and CE. The earlier Tirthankaras, such as Ṛṣabha and Nemi, are primarily known through scriptural narratives and later commentaries, and their dating is not established in the way modern history demands. Jain communities—Digambara and Śvetāmbara, with further sub-traditions—share the same list of Twenty-four Tirthankaras but may differ in certain details of biography, iconography, and ritual emphasis. Despite these differences, the core understanding remains: the Twenty-four Tirthankaras are the supreme exemplars of non-violence, self-restraint, and many-sidedness of truth (anekāntavāda), and their remembered presence shapes Jain ethics, worship, and identity.

In contemporary practice, images of the Twenty-four Tirthankaras are installed in temples, often in series, and their names are recited in liturgical texts and daily prayers. Devotees bow to them not as gods who grant favors but as perfected beings whose qualities they seek to emulate. Festivals such as Mahāvīra Jayantī, Pārśvanātha Jayantī, and special observances linked to Ṛṣabha or Nemi highlight particular Tirthankaras, while the collective memory of all twenty-four reinforces the continuity of Jain dharma across vast stretches of cosmic time. For students and practitioners alike, studying the Twenty-four Tirthankaras is both an entry point into Jain history and a sustained meditation on what it means to live with radical non-violence, discipline, and clarity.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sūtra (Śvetāmbara canonical text)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu
primary_sources.original_text: ṇaṁ se bhagavā mahāvīro vīravāse viharai, sāvatthiṁ nagaraṁ, jettaṇḍe ārāme…
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇaṃ se bhagavā mahāvīro vīravāse viharai, sāvatthiṃ nagaraṃ, jettaṇḍe ārāme…
primary_sources.translation: At that time the Blessed Lord Mahāvīra was staying in the place of Vīra, in the town of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta grove…
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa Sūtra is a Śvetāmbara canonical text recited especially during the Paryuṣaṇa festival. It contains detailed biographies of Mahāvīra and shorter accounts of the other Twenty-four Tirthankaras, outlining their births, renunciations, austerities, omniscience, and nirvāṇa. The passage here illustrates the narrative style used to situate Mahāvīra’s life in specific places and times, while the same text also lists the names and key events of the preceding Tirthankaras.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Canonical text; individual authorship not specified
primary_sources.original_text: je ya ṇaṃ se bhagavanto chaubvisa jinā, te savve kevalī, savvajñā, savvadarasī…
primary_sources.transliteration: je ya ṇaṃ se bhagavanto caubvisa jinā, te savve kevalī, savvajñā, savvadarasī…
primary_sources.translation: Those Blessed Ones, the twenty-four Jinas, all are omniscient, all-knowing, all-seeing…
primary_sources.notes: The Uttarādhyayana Sūtra is an important early doctrinal and narrative text in the Śvetāmbara canon. This type of verse affirms that all Twenty-four Jinas (Tirthankaras) share the same status of omniscience and perfect insight, emphasizing that they are equal in spiritual attainment even though they appear at different times in the cosmic cycle.

primary_sources.title: Tiloya Paṇṇatti (Triloka-prajñapti)
primary_sources.author: Yativṛṣabha (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text: chaubvisa ṇayavvā, ṇāyā ṇāyāṇaṃ, ṇāyāṇaṃ ṇāyā, ṇāyāṇaṃ ṇāyavvā…
primary_sources.transliteration: caubvisa nayavvā, nāyā nāyāṇaṃ, nāyāṇaṃ nāyā, nāyāṇaṃ nāyavvā…
primary_sources.translation: There are twenty-four leaders (Tirthankaras), leaders of leaders, leaders among leaders, leaders for the leaders…
primary_sources.notes: Tiloya Paṇṇatti is a Digambara cosmological text that describes the three worlds and includes lists of the Twenty-four Tirthankaras of each half-cycle. The cited style of verse underscores their role as spiritual leaders who guide beings across saṃsāra. While the exact wording varies by edition, the text is a key source for the systematic enumeration of Tirthankaras in Digambara cosmology.

primary_sources.title: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti)
primary_sources.author: Canonical text; attributed within the Śvetāmbara tradition to the teachings of Mahāvīra
primary_sources.original_text: bhagavā mahāvīro uvāesī: ‘Ṛṣabhādevo paḍhamo tīrthaṅkaro, ajitanāho dūo…’
primary_sources.transliteration: bhagavā mahāvīro uvāesī: ‘Ṛṣabhādevo paḍhamo tīrthaṅkaro, ajitanāho dūo…’
primary_sources.translation: The Blessed Lord Mahāvīra declared: ‘Ṛṣabhadeva is the first Tirthankara, Ajitanātha the second…’
primary_sources.notes: The Bhagavatī Sūtra is a major Śvetāmbara canonical text structured as dialogues between Mahāvīra and his disciples. In sections dealing with cosmology and spiritual lineage, it enumerates the Twenty-four Tirthankaras of the present time-cycle, beginning with Ṛṣabha and ending with Mahāvīra, thereby providing a canonical list that underlies later narrative and iconographic traditions.

primary_sources.title: Inscriptional lists of Tirthankaras (various sites)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous stone inscriptions
primary_sources.original_text: Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Suparśva, Candraprabha…
primary_sources.transliteration: R̥ṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Suparśva, Candraprabha…
primary_sources.translation: Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Suparśva, Candraprabha…
primary_sources.notes: From the early centuries CE onward, Jain inscriptions on pillars, temple walls, and images frequently record partial or complete lists of the Twenty-four Tirthankaras, often in Sanskrit or Prakrit. These epigraphic sources corroborate the canonical list and show its wide acceptance across regions and sects, even though they do not provide detailed biographies.

misconceptions.myth: The Twenty-four Tirthankaras are creator-gods who control the universe and grant worldly favors.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine holds that Tirthankaras are liberated souls who have destroyed all karmic bondage and no longer intervene in worldly affairs. They are revered as teachers and exemplars, not as creators or controllers of the cosmos. Devotional practices focus on emulating their virtues and following their path, rather than seeking miracles or divine intervention.

misconceptions.myth: Mahāvīra founded Jainism and the earlier Tirthankaras are purely mythical additions.
misconceptions.reality: Within Jain tradition, Mahāvīra is the twenty-fourth Tirthankara of the present time-cycle, not the founder of the religion. The existence of earlier Tirthankaras such as Pārśvanātha is supported by relatively early textual and inscriptional evidence, while others are known primarily through scriptural narratives. Modern historical methods cannot verify all details of their lives, but the lineage of Twenty-four Tirthankaras is central to Jain self-understanding and is consistently attested in canonical and later texts.

misconceptions.myth: Different Jain sects have completely different sets of Twenty-four Tirthankaras.
misconceptions.reality: Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, along with their sub-sects, share the same list of Twenty-four Tirthankaras for the present time-cycle, from Ṛṣabhanātha to Mahāvīra. Sectarian differences concern aspects such as canonical status of certain texts, details of biography, iconographic conventions, and ritual practices, but not the basic enumeration or spiritual status of the Twenty-four Tirthankaras.

misconceptions.myth: The symbols (lāñchanas) of the Tirthankaras are arbitrary decorative motifs without doctrinal meaning.
misconceptions.reality: The symbols associated with each Tirthankara function as identifiers in art and ritual and are rooted in scriptural and narrative traditions. They are linked to auspicious dreams, birthmarks, or specific episodes in the Tirthankara’s life and serve as mnemonic devices for remembering their qualities and stories. While not doctrinal in the sense of philosophical propositions, they are integral to the way Jain communities visualize and recall the Twenty-four Tirthankaras.
